collisions-s1.title: Collision trials with two carts
collisions-s1.text: In each trial a 0.40 kg cart A rolls into a 0.60 kg cart B at rest on a level, low-friction track. Motion sensors record the velocities just before and just after. Positive is to the right.

collisions-s2.title: Two carts that stick
collisions-s2.html: The track is level and friction is negligible. Positive is to the right.

items.q: In which trials is the total momentum of the two carts the same before and after?
options: In each of the three trials
In trial 1, the elastic one, and not the others
In trial 3, where the carts stick, and not the others
In no trial, because the carts' speeds change
Right: every trial gives 0.40 kg·m/s after, as before.
Momentum is conserved in every collision with no net external force, elastic or not.
Sticking does not make momentum special; check the products in trials 1 and 2 too.
The individual speeds change, but the total momentum does not.
Trial 2
Trial 1
Trial 3
Each of the three, because momentum is conserved in each

why.correct: K before = ½(0.40)(1.00)² = 0.20 J. After: trial 1, 0.20 J (elastic); trial 2, 0.11 J (inelastic); trial 3, 0.080 J (perfectly inelastic).
options: K after = 0.002 + 0.108 = 0.11 J, less than 0.20 J: inelastic.
Right: K after = ½(0.40)(0.20)² + ½(0.60)(0.80)² = 0.20 J, equal to K before.
The carts stick, which is perfectly inelastic: K drops to 0.080 J.
Conserving momentum does not make a collision elastic. Elastic means total K is unchanged too.

items.q: How much kinetic energy is converted to other forms in trial 3, in joules?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the kinetic energy after. Subtract it from the 0.20 J before.

why.correct: Before: 0.20 J. After: ½(1.00 kg)(0.40 m/s)² = 0.080 J. Converted: 0.12 J, to thermal energy and sound as the Velcro grips.

items.q: In trial 1, cart A bounces back. Did cart A's own kinetic energy stay the same?
options: Yes: in an elastic collision each cart keeps its kinetic energy
Yes: A moves back with its original speed
No: A gave most of its K to B; the total stayed 0.20 J
No: the total kinetic energy went down

why.correct: In an elastic collision the total kinetic energy is the same before and after, but energy moves between the objects.
options: Elastic means the total K is unchanged; individual kinetic energies can change.
A moves back at 0.20 m/s, much slower than 1.00 m/s.
Right: K_A falls from 0.20 J to 0.008 J; B gains 0.192 J.
Trial 1 is elastic: the total stayed 0.20 J.

items.q: Trial 3 is repeated with cart B loaded to 1.60 kg. Compared with the original trial 3, the speed of the stuck carts after the collision is
options: the same, because A has the same momentum
one quarter as large
twice as large
one half as large
The same momentum is now shared by twice the total mass.
B's mass is a little under 3 times larger, but the total mass (which matters) doubles.
Adding mass to the stuck pair slows it down.

items.q: What is the velocity of the stuck carts just after the collision, in m/s? Include the sign.

mistakes.why: Value: B moves left, so its momentum is negative: (1.0)(−1.5).
Value: averaging velocities ignores the masses. Use total momentum over total mass.

items.q: How much kinetic energy does the system lose in the collision, in joules?

mistakes.why: Value: kinetic energies do not cancel. B's 1.1 J adds to A's 9.0 J even though B moves left.

why.correct: Before: ½(2.0)(3.0)² + ½(1.0)(1.5)² = 9.0 J + 1.125 J = 10.125 J. After: ½(3.0)(1.5)² = 3.375 J. Lost: 6.75 J, about 6.8 J (to thermal energy and sound).

items.q: A student finds the final velocity by setting the kinetic energy before equal to the kinetic energy after. What is wrong?
options: K is not conserved when carts stick; start from momentum
Nothing: kinetic energy is conserved in a collision like this one
The student should have used the carts' weights instead of masses
Kinetic energy gives the speed but not the direction, so add a sign

why.correct: In every collision on a frictionless track momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is conserved only if the collision is elastic. When objects stick, start from momentum.
options: Right: start from momentum, which is conserved because no net external force acts.
Kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions. Sticking is the opposite extreme.
Weights would not fix the method; kinetic energy is simply not conserved here.
The magnitude would still be wrong, because K is not conserved.

items.q: Which momentum bar chart (bars for A, B and the total, before and after) is correct?
options: Before: A +6.0, B +1.5, total +7.5; after: total +7.5
Before: A +6.0, B −1.5, total +4.5; after: A and B together +4.5
Before: A +6.0, B −1.5, total +4.5; after: 0, because the carts stop
Before: A +3.0, B −1.5, total +1.5; after: +1.5

why.correct: Momenta in kg·m/s: A = (2.0)(3.0) = +6.0, B = (1.0)(−1.5) = −1.5. Total +4.5 before and after.
options: B moves left, so its bar points below zero (−1.5).
Right: the total bar is the same before and after.
The carts move on together at +1.5 m/s; the total stays +4.5.
These are velocities, not momenta. Multiply by each mass.

items.q: Which is true of every collision between two objects on a level, frictionless surface?
options: Total kinetic energy is conserved; momentum may or may not be
Both total momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved
Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy may or may not be
Neither is conserved, because the objects push on each other

why.correct: Momentum: conserved whenever the net external force is zero. Kinetic energy: conserved only in elastic collisions.
options: This swaps them. Momentum is the one that is always conserved here.
True only for elastic collisions.
Right: no net external force, so p is constant; K is constant only if elastic.
The pushes are internal; they cannot change the total momentum.

items.q: A collision in which the total kinetic energy after is less than before, but the objects do not stick together, is
options: elastic
perfectly inelastic
an explosion
inelastic

why.correct: Elastic: K unchanged. Inelastic: K decreases. Perfectly inelastic: K decreases the most possible, and the objects stick.
options: Elastic means no loss of total kinetic energy.
Perfectly inelastic means the objects stick and move together.
In an explosion kinetic energy increases, from stored energy.
Right: some kinetic energy became other forms, but the objects separate.

items.q: A 1500 kg car moving at 12 m/s rear-ends a 1000. kg car at rest, and they lock bumpers. How fast do they move just after, in m/s?

mistakes.why: Value: that comes from conserving kinetic energy. Locked bumpers make it perfectly inelastic; use momentum.

items.q: A ball of clay and a rubber ball, of equal mass and speed, each hit a block. Which one is more likely to knock the block over?
options: The rubber ball, because a bounce gives a larger impulse
The clay, because it hands its whole energy to the block
Both equally, because they have the same momentum
The clay, because sticking is an elastic collision

why.correct: The block's impulse equals the ball's change in momentum (opposite). Clay: Δp = mv. Rubber ball bouncing back: up to 2mv.
options: Right: reversing the ball's momentum takes more impulse than stopping it.
Knocking over depends on the push (impulse). The bounce delivers more.
Same initial momentum, but different changes: the bounce changes it more.
Sticking is perfectly inelastic, not elastic.

items.q: Two identical carts, one moving at v and one at rest, collide on a frictionless track. Which outcome is impossible?
options: The first cart stops and the second moves at v
Both carts move forward at v
They stick and then move together at v/2
The first moves at v/4 and the second at 3v/4

why.correct: Any outcome must keep the total momentum at mv, and the total K cannot rise without a stored energy source. Both moving at v breaks momentum conservation.
options: Possible: momentum mv is conserved and K is unchanged (elastic).
Right: the total momentum would double, from mv to 2mv.
Possible: momentum mv is conserved (perfectly inelastic).
Possible: momentum mv is conserved and K drops (inelastic).

items.q: Two carts on a frictionless track collide and stick together. For the two-cart system, compare just after with just before.

variables.name: Total momentum
variables.why: No net external force acts during the collision.

variables.name: Total kinetic energy
variables.why: Sticking is perfectly inelastic; some K becomes thermal energy and sound.

variables.name: Thermal energy of the carts
variables.why: The kinetic energy lost is converted, mostly to thermal energy.

why.correct: Momentum first: it is unchanged. Energy second: the total is conserved, but kinetic energy decreases.
